entries.meaning: The mockery of the wicked will benefit me: crows call the cuckoo harsh, cranes laugh at swans and frogs at the rain-thirsty cātaka; the stained wicked laugh at spotless speech. Those fond of poetry but without love for Rāma’s feet will at least enjoy its comic flavour. My vernacular composition and simple mind deserve laughter; laughter carries no blame. The story seems dull to those who neither understand nor cherish the Lord’s feet, but to uncontentious minds devoted to Hari and Hara the story of Raghubara is sweet. Good people, knowing the heart adorned with devotion to Rāma, will listen and praise its fair speech. I am no poet, not skilled in expression, and lack all arts and learning. I know none of the letters, meanings, ornaments, metres, structures, modes of feeling, many rasas, or kinds of poetic merit and fault. I state this truth on blank paper. My composition lacks every merit except one known throughout the world; considering that one merit, clear-minded listeners will hear it.

Within this composition is the noble name of Raghupati, supremely purifying and the essence of Purāṇa and Veda. It is the abode of auspiciousness and destroyer of misfortune, the name that Śiva repeats with Umā. Even an ingenious work by a fine poet lacks beauty without Rāma’s name, just as a moon-faced woman adorned in every way does not shine without clothing. But the words of a poor poet, though devoid of every merit, are respectfully recited and heard by the wise when marked by Rāma’s name; saints gather virtues like bees gather nectar. Though the poem has not one poetic flavour, Rāma’s majesty is manifest within it. This assurance came to my mind: whom has good company not ennobled? Even smoke abandons its natural acridity and, in the company of agarwood, carries fragrance. My expression is rustic, but the subject it describes—the story of Rāma—brings auspiciousness to the world.

A jewel, ruby or pearl does not shine so splendidly while in a serpent’s hood, mountain or elephant’s head; placed in a king’s crown or on a young woman’s body, each gains its fullest beauty. Likewise, the wise say, a fine poet’s composition is born in one place and acquires manifold beauty elsewhere. For the sake of devotion Sarasvatī leaves Brahmā’s abode and comes running when remembered; yet without bathing in the lake of Rāma’s deeds, even her toil cannot be removed by ten million remedies. Understanding this, learned poets sing Hari’s fame, which removes the impurity of Kali. When speech has been used to praise an ordinary person, it beats its head and regrets it. The heart is the ocean, understanding the shell, and Sarasvatī the Svāti rain, say the wise: if excellent water in the form of reflection falls, beautiful pearl-like poems arise. Pierced by poetic skill and strung on the excellent thread of Rāma’s story, saints wear them with great love upon their pure hearts.

Those born in this terrible age act like crows while dressed as swans. They follow wrong roads, abandon the Vedic path, wear deceit as their body and serve as vessels of Kali’s impurity. They call themselves devotees of Rāma but are servants of gold, anger and desire. Among them I stand first in the world’s rank, a bold hypocrite and leader of this trade. If I told all my faults, the narrative would grow and I would never reach its end; therefore I have named very few, from which the discerning will understand the rest. Understanding my petition in its various ways, no one should find fault after hearing the story. Anyone who still doubts it is more inert and intellectually poor than I. I am no poet and claim no cleverness; I sing Rāma’s virtues according to my understanding. How boundless are Raghupati’s deeds, and how worldly my mind! When wind can blow Mount Meru away, what account is taken of cotton? Contemplating Rāma’s immeasurable lordship, my mind trembles greatly while telling the story. Sarasvatī, Śeṣa, Śiva, Brahmā, Āgamas, Vedas and Purāṇas ceaselessly sing his qualities while saying, ‘not this, not this.’

The Lord alone knows his own lordship, yet no one can refrain from speaking of it. The Veda explains the reason: devotion’s power is expressed in many ways. The One is desireless, formless, nameless, unborn, being-consciousness-bliss and the supreme abode, all-pervading and universal in form; yet that Lord assumed a body and performed many deeds solely for devotees’ welfare. Supremely compassionate and loving toward those who surrender, he has extraordinary tenderness for his people, never becomes angry with them, restores what is lost, favours the poor, and is the guileless, mighty master Raghurāja. Knowing this, the wise describe Hari’s fame and make their own speech pure and fruitful. Relying on that strength, I shall bow my head at Rāma’s feet and tell Raghupati’s virtues. The sages first sang Hari’s fame; walking on their path is easy for me. Even an ant, extremely small, can cross a very great river without labour once a king has had a bridge built across it.

Showing my mind this source of strength, I shall compose the lovely story of Raghupati. I bow at the lotus feet of Vyāsa and the many foremost poets who reverently described Hari’s fair fame; may they fulfil all my wishes. I salute the poets of this age who narrated Raghupati’s multitude of virtues, and the supremely wise vernacular poets who told Hari’s deeds in the people’s language. I bow without deceit to all who have been, now are, or will be. Be gracious and grant the boon that the assembly of saints honour this composition, for a work the wise do not esteem is wasted labour undertaken by a childish poet. Only that fame, poetry and prosperity are good which, like Gaṅgā, benefit everyone. Yet Rāma’s fame is excellent and my expression rustic: this mismatch troubles me. By your grace even that union can succeed for me, like fine embroidery making coarse cloth pleasing. The discerning esteem simple poetry of stainless renown when even an enemy, forgetting natural hostility, hears and praises it. That is impossible without a pure mind, and my intellectual power is very slight; be gracious so I may tell Hari’s fame—I petition again and again. O poet-swans who dwell beautifully in the lake of Raghubara’s deeds, hear this child’s plea, see its sincere aspiration and be gracious to me. I bow at the lotus feet of the sage Vālmīki, who composed the Rāmāyaṇa, at once firm and tender, beautiful, free of faults and containing Dūṣaṇa. I bow to all four Vedas, like boats upon the ocean of becoming, who feel no weariness even in dreams while describing Raghubara’s stainless fame. I bow to the dust of Brahmā’s feet, who made the ocean of worldly existence wherein saints, nectar, moon and wish-granting cow appeared alongside the wicked, poison and wine. Bowing to the feet of gods, Brahmins, the wise and planets, I join my hands: be gracious and fulfil all my lovely aspirations.

Again I bow to Sarasvatī and the river Gaṅgā, whose twin histories are purifying and beautiful. One removes sin by bathing and drinking; the other removes ignorance through speaking and hearing. I salute the teacher, father, mother, Śiva and Bhavānī, friends of the humble and daily givers. To Tulsī they are in every way servant and master, friend, and Sītā’s Lord, offering unconditional welfare. Seeing Kali, Śiva and Girijā created for the world’s good a network of Śābara mantras: their syllables do not match, their meaning and recitation are obscure, yet their power is manifest through Śiva’s majesty. May that Lord of Umā be favourable to me and make this story the root of joy and auspiciousness. Remembering Śivā and Śiva and receiving their grace, I describe Rāma’s deeds with delight in my heart. Through Śiva’s grace my composition shines like a night adorned by the company of the moon. Those who tell, hear and attentively understand this story with love will become devoted to Rāma’s feet, free from Kali’s stain and heirs to great auspiciousness. If Hara and Gaurī’s grace toward me is true even in a dream, may everything I have said about this vernacular composition’s power come true.

I bow to the supremely holy city of Ayodhyā and the Sarayū river, destroyer of Kali’s stain. Again I salute the city’s men and women, for whom the Lord has no slight affection. He destroyed the flood of sin belonging to Sītā’s detractors and, making them free of sorrow, settled them in his realm. I bow to Kausalyā, the eastern horizon whose fame pervades the whole world, where the lovely moon Raghupati rose—delighting the universe and freezing the lotuses of the wicked. I honour king Daśaratha and all the queens as embodiments of merit and auspiciousness. I salute them in deed, mind and speech; knowing me as their son’s servant, may they show grace. By creating them even the Creator became great: they are the utmost reach of glory, Rāma’s father and mother. I bow to Ayodhyā’s king, whose love for Rāma’s feet was true; when separated from his beloved, that Friend of the humble, he discarded his dear body like straw.
